files.note: The heart of sync. Push validates a batch and upserts it under an advisory lock; Pull merges tables by server_seq and pages with has_more.
files.summary:
Package store implements the sync protocol on top of Postgres.

Clients push batches of changed records and pull everything with a
server_seq above their cursor. Each entity type gets its own table and its
own field in Changes; adding a type means adding a migration, a struct with
upsert/pull functions, and wiring it into Push and Pull below.

symbols.doc: Origins a record can come from.

symbols.name: Changes
symbols.doc: Changes is a set of records grouped by entity type.

symbols.name: PushResult
symbols.doc:
PushResult says which records were written and which were skipped because
the server already had an equal or newer version.

symbols.name: PullResult
symbols.doc:
PullResult is one page of changes. Cursor is the value to send as "since"
on the next pull.

symbols.name: ValidationError
symbols.doc: ValidationError marks a request the client must fix; the API maps it to 400.

symbols.name: Store
symbols.doc: Store is the Postgres-backed sync store.

symbols.name: (Changes) Validate
symbols.doc: Validate checks every record in the batch before anything is written.

symbols.name: (*Store) Push
symbols.doc: Push writes a batch atomically.

symbols.name: (*Store) Pull
symbols.doc:
Pull returns up to limit records changed after since, across all types,
in server_seq order.

files.summary:
Every synced write takes the next value from this sequence. Clients pull

symbols.name: sync_seq
symbols.doc:
Every synced write takes the next value from this sequence. Clients pull

files.source:
-- Every synced write takes the next value from this sequence. Clients pull
-- "everything with server_seq > cursor", which avoids relying on device clocks.
CREATE SEQUENCE sync_seq;

CREATE TABLE fasts (
    id           uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    started_at   timestamptz NOT NULL,
    ended_at     timestamptz,
    goal_seconds integer     NOT NULL CHECK (goal_seconds > 0),
    notes        text        NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL,
    updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL,
    deleted_at   timestamptz,
    origin       text        NOT NULL,
    server_seq   bigint      NOT NULL DEFAULT nextval('sync_seq'),
    CHECK (ended_at IS NULL OR ended_at >= started_at)
);

CREATE INDEX fasts_server_seq_idx ON fasts (server_seq);

files.note: Two-stage build: cross-compile on the build machine, ship a distroless image.
files.summary:
Cross-compiles on the build machine (e.g. an arm64 Mac) for the target
platform (linux/amd64 on the Synology).
files.source:
# Cross-compiles on the build machine (e.g. an arm64 Mac) for the target
# platform (linux/amd64 on the Synology).
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.27 AS build
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH \
    go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/api ./cmd/api

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/api /api
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]

# Coach backend. Nothing here publishes a port on the LAN: the only way in is
# the tailnet, through the `ts` container (hostname "coach").
name: coach

services:
  ts:
    image: tailscale/tailscale:stable
    hostname: coach
    environment:
      TS_AUTHKEY: ${TS_AUTHKEY:?set TS_AUTHKEY in .env}
      TS_STATE_DIR: /var/lib/tailscale
      TS_SERVE_CONFIG: /config/serve.json
    volumes:
      - ${DATA_DIR:-./data}/tailscale:/var/lib/tailscale
      - ./serve.json:/config/serve.json:ro
    restart: unless-stopped

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    container_name: coach-db
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: coach
      POSTGRES_USER: coach
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}
    volumes:
      - ${DATA_DIR:-./data}/postgres:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U coach -d coach"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20
    restart: unless-stopped

  api:
    # On the NAS this image is loaded from build-image.sh (it can't build
    # there). Elsewhere, compose builds it if it's missing.
    image: coach-api:latest
    build: ../server
    # Shares the ts container's network, so tailscale serve reaches it on
    # 127.0.0.1:8080 and it reaches Postgres as "db".
    network_mode: service:ts
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://coach:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/coach?sslmode=disable
      COACH_API_TOKEN: ${COACH_API_TOKEN:?set COACH_API_TOKEN in .env}
      LISTEN_ADDR: 127.0.0.1:8080
    depends_on:
      ts:
        condition: service_started
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped

Builds the amd64 API image on the Mac (the NAS can't build) and optionally ships and restarts it.
files.summary:
Builds the API image for the NAS (linux/amd64) on this machine.

Synology's kernel lacks seccomp, which Docker's builder needs for RUN steps,
so images can't be built on the NAS. They run there fine.

./build-image.sh                 # writes dist/coach-api.tar
./build-image.sh user@nas-host   # also copies it over, loads it and
# restarts the project (asks for sudo)

REMOTE_DIR overrides where the project lives on the NAS.
files.source:
#!/bin/sh
# Builds the API image for the NAS (linux/amd64) on this machine.
#
# Synology's kernel lacks seccomp, which Docker's builder needs for RUN steps,
# so images can't be built on the NAS. They run there fine.
#
#   ./build-image.sh                 # writes dist/coach-api.tar
#   ./build-image.sh user@nas-host   # also copies it over, loads it and
#                                    # restarts the project (asks for sudo)
#
# REMOTE_DIR overrides where the project lives on the NAS.
set -eu
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

mkdir -p dist
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 -t coach-api:latest \
  --output type=docker,dest=dist/coach-api.tar ../server
echo "built dist/coach-api.tar"

[ $# -eq 0 ] && exit 0

NAS=$1
REMOTE_DIR=${REMOTE_DIR:-/volume1/docker/coach/deploy}
DOCKER=/usr/local/bin/docker # not on sudo's PATH on DSM

# -O: legacy scp protocol, which works without enabling SFTP in DSM.
scp -O dist/coach-api.tar "$NAS:$REMOTE_DIR/coach-api.tar"
ssh -t "$NAS" "sudo $DOCKER load -i $REMOTE_DIR/coach-api.tar \
  && rm $REMOTE_DIR/coach-api.tar \
  && cd $REMOTE_DIR && sudo $DOCKER compose up -d"

files.note: Nightly pg_dump with 30-day retention.
files.summary:
Nightly Postgres dump. On the Synology, run it from
Control Panel > Task Scheduler as root, e.g.:
/volume1/docker/coach/deploy/backup.sh /volume1/backups/coach
and include that folder in a Hyper Backup task for an off-box copy.
files.source:
#!/bin/sh
# Nightly Postgres dump. On the Synology, run it from
# Control Panel > Task Scheduler as root, e.g.:
#   /volume1/docker/coach/deploy/backup.sh /volume1/backups/coach
# and include that folder in a Hyper Backup task for an off-box copy.
set -eu

BACKUP_DIR=${1:?usage: backup.sh <backup-dir> [keep-days]}
KEEP_DAYS=${2:-30}

mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"
out="$BACKUP_DIR/coach-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).dump"

# Custom format (-Fc) is compressed and restores with pg_restore.
docker exec coach-db pg_dump -U coach -d coach -Fc > "$out.tmp"
mv "$out.tmp" "$out"

find "$BACKUP_DIR" -name 'coach-*.dump' -mtime +"$KEEP_DAYS" -delete
echo "wrote $out"

# Use a reusable or pre-approved key, and tag it if you use ACL tags.

files.source:
# Deploying the backend

Three containers: Tailscale (`ts`), Postgres (`db`) and the Go API (`api`).
Nothing is published on the LAN. Clients reach the server at
`https://coach.<your-tailnet>.ts.net` over Tailscale.

## One-time Tailscale setup

1. In the Tailscale admin console, enable **MagicDNS** and **HTTPS certificates** (DNS page).
2. Create an auth key (Settings > Keys) and put it in `.env` as `TS_AUTHKEY`.
3. Install Tailscale on the iPhone and the laptop, signed in to the same tailnet.

## Synology (DS2419+II, DSM 7.2)

1. Install **Container Manager** from Package Center.
2. Copy the repo to the NAS, e.g. `/volume1/docker/coach` (the `server/` and `deploy/` folders are what's needed).
3. In `deploy/`, `cp .env.example .env` and fill it in. Set `DATA_DIR=/volume1/docker/coach/data`.
4. Build the API image **on the Mac** and load it onto the NAS (enable SSH in Control Panel > Terminal first):

   ```sh
   deploy/build-image.sh you@nas-hostname
   ```

   This cross-builds for linux/amd64, copies the image over, loads it and runs
   `docker compose up -d`. It asks for your NAS password for sudo.
   Without an argument it only writes `deploy/dist/coach-api.tar`, which you can
   load through Container Manager > Image > Add > From file instead.

   **Don't build on the NAS.** DSM's kernel has no seccomp support, so
   `docker compose up --build` (or a Container Manager project build) fails with
   `seccomp: config provided but seccomp not supported`. Running containers works fine.
5. Check it's up from the laptop: `curl https://coach.<tailnet>.ts.net/healthz` should return `{"status":"ok"}`.
   The first request can take a few seconds while the certificate is issued.
6. Schedule `backup.sh` (see the comment at the top of it).

To deploy a new API version later, run `deploy/build-image.sh you@nas-hostname` again.

## Local development (Mac)

Use the same compose file with Docker Desktop running and a separate auth key
(it shows up as another `coach` node, e.g. `coach-1`). Or run only Postgres
and the API directly:

```sh
docker run -d --name coach-dev-db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 postgres:17
cd server
DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:dev@localhost:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable \
COACH_API_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32) go run ./cmd/api
```

Integration tests need a disposable database. They drop the schema:

```sh
COACH_TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:dev@localhost:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable go test ./...
```

## Analysis access

Postgres is forwarded on the tailnet at `coach.<tailnet>.ts.net:5432`, for
psql, Python notebooks and the like. Consider creating a read-only role for
analysis, separate from the `coach` user the API uses.

## Moving to a Mac mini later

Stop the project, copy `DATA_DIR` and `.env`, and run `docker compose up -d`
on the new machine. The tailnet name stays `coach` as long as the `tailscale`
state directory comes along.

symbols.name: nowMillis
symbols.doc:
Now, at whole-millisecond precision. Every timestamp the app writes
goes through this so it survives SQLite (integer ms), JSON (3 digits)
and Postgres (µs) round trips exactly, which last-writer-wins
comparisons rely on.

symbols.name: truncatedToMillis
symbols.doc:
Rounds to the nearest millisecond. Rounding (not flooring) keeps this
idempotent: k/1000 as a Double can sit just below k ms, and flooring
it again would lose a millisecond.

# XcodeGen spec. Regenerate the Xcode project after editing:
#   cd ios && xcodegen
name: Coach
options:
  bundleIdPrefix: dev.coach
  deploymentTarget:
    iOS: "27.0"
  createIntermediateGroups: true

settings:
  base:
    SWIFT_VERSION: "6.0"
    MARKETING_VERSION: "0.1.0"
    CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION: "1"
    DEVELOPMENT_TEAM: "" # set your team ID to run on a device

packages:
  GRDB:
    url: https://github.com/groue/GRDB.swift
    from: 7.0.0

targets:
  Coach:
    type: application
    platform: iOS
    sources:

# Coach iOS app

SwiftUI, iOS 27+. The Xcode project is generated from `project.yml`; don't edit
`Coach.xcodeproj` by hand.

```sh
cd ios
xcodegen                     # after adding/removing files or changing project.yml
open Coach.xcodeproj
xcodebuild test -project Coach.xcodeproj -scheme Coach \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17'
```

## Layout

- `Coach/Theme`: NEON//OS design system (colors, fonts, chamfer shapes, panels,
  segmented bars, buttons, grid and scanlines).
- `Coach/Data`: GRDB database. Timestamps are stored as integer milliseconds so
  they round-trip exactly; sync's last-writer-wins depends on that.
- `Coach/Sync`: push queued changes, then pull past the cursor. Same conflict
  rule as the server.
- `Coach/Features`: screens.

## Connecting to the server

Settings (gear on Today) > UPLINK: enter `https://coach.<tailnet>.ts.net` and
the `COACH_API_TOKEN` from `deploy/.env`, then TEST LINK. The token is kept in
the Keychain. The simulator uses the Mac's network, so it reaches the server
whenever the Mac is on the tailnet.

## Running on your iPhone

Set `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` in `project.yml` (and change the `dev.coach.*` bundle IDs
if you like), run `xcodegen`, then build to the device from Xcode.

# Coach — Spec (draft 2)

A personal fitness app for one user: workouts, fasting, health metrics, and later diet. The data lives in a backend the user owns. A laptop, a web UI or an LLM can read it and write to it. The original notes are in `inital_spec.md`.

## Decisions so far

| Area | Decision |
|---|---|
| Platform | Native SwiftUI iPhone app, plus a minimal Apple Watch companion that arrives with lifting |
| Storage | Local-first: SQLite on the device, and the app works fully offline |
| Sync | Opportunistic background sync to a home server reached over Tailscale |
| Backend | Postgres plus a small HTTP API on the home server. Keep the schema portable so it can move to managed Postgres (e.g. Supabase) later |
| Languages | iOS/watchOS: Swift (SwiftUI). API and MCP server: Go. Web app: TypeScript. Ad-hoc analysis: Python against Postgres |
| Home server | Synology DS2419+II for now (x86, Docker via Container Manager; Tailscale runs as a container). May move to a Mac mini later, so everything runs in containers |
| Units | Both. Store SI units internally; imperial or metric is a display preference |
| Export | None for now (no Strava, FIT export and the like) |
| Source of truth | The backend. HealthKit is imported into it, and the app's own workouts are written back to HealthKit |
| LLM integration | An MCP server on the home server, so Claude Desktop / Claude Code can query history and write plans |
| Desktop | A web app served from the home server, reachable over Tailscale |
| Workouts | Structured (intervals, sets, segments), built one type at a time, cycling first |
| Trainer | Record only in v1. The design leaves room for ERG / target control later |
| Fasting v1 | Start/stop, a timer, a goal, notifications. No history, widgets or Live Activity yet |
| Diet v1 | Fasting only. Diet logging comes later |
| Lifting | Sets logged live, on the Watch where possible, otherwise on the phone |
| Running | Both outdoor (GPS) and treadmill (Bluetooth FTMS where available) |
| Visual style | Retro "NEON//OS": chamfered panels, purple grid, glowing cyan/magenta/amber, segmented bars, monospace data, text-only tab bar. Scanlines are a user setting (on by default) |

Mockups: https://claude.ai/artifact/96T2a41yw2PCG3S9DBhFs4 (the second row is the chosen direction)

## Architecture

```
 iPhone app (SwiftUI)                 Home server (on the tailnet only)
 ┌───────────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────────────┐
 │ UI                    │            │ HTTP API  ──┐                │
 │ Recording engine      │   sync     │ MCP server ─┼─> Postgres     │
 │ BLE sensor layer      │ <────────> │ Web app  ───┘                │
 │ HealthKit bridge      │ (Tailscale)│ Backups                      │
 │ SQLite + sync outbox  │            └──────────────────────────────┘
 └──────────┬────────────┘                  ^               ^
            │ WatchConnectivity             │ Tailscale     │ MCP (stdio/HTTP)
 ┌──────────┴────────────┐            Laptop browser    Claude Desktop / Code
 │ Watch app (later)     │
 └───────────────────────┘
```

### iOS app
- **Local DB:** SQLite through GRDB. GRDB gives explicit SQL and migrations, and that control makes the sync logic simpler than it would be with SwiftData.
- **Sensors (CoreBluetooth):** standard GATT profiles: Heart Rate (0x180D), Cycling Power (0x1818), Cycling Speed & Cadence (0x1816), and Fitness Machine / FTMS (0x1826) for trainers and treadmills. FTMS is also the way to control a trainer later.
- **Tymewear:** the VitalPro HR strap is a normal BLE/ANT+ heart-rate strap. The breathing sensor is BLE-only and uses a proprietary, undocumented service: Garmin and Wahoo support it through vendor integrations, not a standard profile. See *Tymewear plan* below.
- **Background:** the `bluetooth-central` background mode keeps a recording going with the screen locked. Save samples to disk as they arrive so a crash doesn't lose the ride.
- **HealthKit:** import sleep, HRV, resting HR, weight and workouts recorded by other apps. Export finished workouts with HR and energy.
- **Notifications:** scheduled locally on the device, such as the fasting goal, T-minus alerts and workout reminders. No push server is needed.

### Sync model
- Every row has a client-generated UUID, `created_at`, `updated_at`, a `deleted_at` tombstone and an `origin` (`phone`, `watch`, `web`, `mcp`).
- The phone keeps an **outbox** of local changes and pushes them when the server is reachable. It pulls everything changed since the last sync cursor.
- Conflicts are resolved last-writer-wins per record. There's little to conflict over in practice: recordings come from the phone, and plans mostly come from the desktop or MCP.
- Plan changes made off the phone show up as an **"incoming changes" review** in the app, not as silent edits.
- Sample streams (per-second power, HR, cadence, breathing) are stored as compressed chunks per recording instead of one row per sample.

### Backend
- Go services: the HTTP API and the MCP server (official Go MCP SDK), sharing one data-access package. Each is a single static binary in a small container.
- Deployment: Docker Compose on the Synology (Postgres, API, MCP server, web app), with data on a NAS volume. The same compose file moves to a Mac mini unchanged.
- Plain Postgres with nothing vendor-specific, so moving to Supabase later is just a data migration.
- Network: a Tailscale container in the Compose project joins the tailnet as `coach` and serves HTTPS (with a real certificate, which iOS requires) to the API. Postgres is forwarded on the tailnet for analysis tools. Nothing is published on the LAN.
- Auth: a bearer token for now, with Tailscale providing the network-level security. Per-device tokens can come later.
- Backups: a nightly `pg_dump` to a NAS share, picked up by Synology Hyper Backup for an off-box copy.

### MCP server
Starting tools:
- `get_profile` / `update_profile` (FTP, HR zones, weight)
- `list_workouts(from, to, type)` and `get_workout(id)`, including summaries and downsampled streams
- `get_metrics(kind, from, to)` for sleep, HRV, resting HR, fasting
- `create_plan`, `update_plan`, `schedule_workout`, validated against the workout schema
- `get_schema(type)`, so the LLM always writes valid structured workouts

Privacy note: anything the MCP tools return goes to the LLM provider during that session. Tools should return summaries by default and full streams only when asked.

## Structured workouts

There's one JSON schema per workout type, and it's both the storage format and what an LLM writes. Cycling comes first. Here is a draft:

```json
{
  "type": "cycling",
  "schema_version": 1,
  "name": "Sweet Spot 3x12",
  "target_basis": "ftp_fraction",
  "steps": [
    { "kind": "warmup",   "duration_s": 600, "power": { "from": 0.50, "to": 0.75 } },
    { "kind": "repeat", "count": 3, "steps": [
      { "kind": "work",     "duration_s": 720, "power": { "low": 0.88, "high": 0.93 }, "cadence": { "low": 85, "high": 95 } },
      { "kind": "recovery", "duration_s": 300, "power": { "value": 0.55 } }
    ]},
    { "kind": "cooldown", "duration_s": 600, "power": { "from": 0.65, "to": 0.45 } }
  ],
  "notes": "Stay seated, smooth cadence."
}
```

- Targets are fractions of FTP, resolved against the profile when the ride starts. This keeps old plans valid after an FTP change. The profile keeps an FTP history.
- Each step can have alerts, such as a cue a few seconds before the next step.
- Lifting (sets × reps × load / RPE), running (segments by time or distance, with pace or HR targets) and mobility (holds and flows) get their own schemas when we reach them.

## Tymewear plan

The breathing data (breath rate, tidal volume, minute ventilation) is the only sensor without a public protocol. Try these in order:

1. **Ask Tymewear.** They already integrate with Garmin, Wahoo and Apple Watch, so a partner or developer BLE spec exists. Email support or partnerships and ask for the breathing sensor's GATT service and data format for a personal app.
2. **Inspect your own device.** Use a BLE explorer (nRF Connect or LightBlue) to list its services and characteristics, and see whether the notifications are readable. Only for personal use with your own device, and check Tymewear's terms first.
3. **Fallback:** record breathing through Tymewear's own path (their app, or Garmin/Wahoo, which write breathing fields into the FIT file), then import that file afterwards and merge it onto the ride by timestamp. Live breathing would then be missing from the ride screen, but the data would still reach the backend.

The sensor layer treats Tymewear as an optional plugin, so cycling recording doesn't wait on this.

## Data model sketch (v1)

- `profile`: FTP history, HR zones, display units (imperial/metric)
- `fast`: start, end, goal duration, notes
- `workout_plan`: type, JSON body, `schema_version`, origin
- `scheduled_workout`: plan id, date/time, status (planned / done / skipped)
- `recording`: type, start, end, scheduled_workout id, summary stats, sensors used, HealthKit UUID
- `recording_stream`: recording id, channel (power / hr / cadence / breath_rate / ventilation / gps), compressed chunk
- `metric_sample`: kind (sleep, hrv, rhr, weight…), timestamp, value, source
- `sensor_device`: BLE identifier, type, name, last seen

## Milestones

1. **Foundation:** Xcode project; design-system components (chamfered panel, segmented bar, glowing text, tab bar); GRDB setup; home server running Postgres and the API; Tailscale; one entity syncing end to end.
2. **Fasting:** start/stop, goal, notifications, the Today card. Synced.
3. **Cycling recording:** BLE pairing; HR, power, cadence and FTMS data; Tymewear if feasible; the live ride screen; save, export to HealthKit, sync streams.
4. **Structured cycling:** the schema; the plan calendar (Train tab); running a workout with targets shown (no ERG); the MCP server with plan tools; the incoming-changes review.
5. **Health import:** HealthKit sleep / HRV / RHR into the Body tab and the Today vitals.
6. **Web app v1:** calendar, plan editor, ride analysis charts.

Later, roughly in order: ERG / trainer control; lifting plus the Watch app; running (GPS plus treadmill); mobility; diet logging; Live Activities and widgets.

## Open questions

- Synology model: Container Manager needs a supported (mostly x86 "+" series) model.
- Tymewear: the answer from Tymewear, or what a BLE scan shows.
- Web framework (React, Svelte…), to decide at milestone 6.
- Minimum iOS version: assume the newest only.

# Goal
I would like to build a workout and fitness application for myself. The goal is to have a place where I can handle multiple exercise, health, fasting, potentially diet, sleep, and other pieces of information as well. One thing  really want is for the data to not just live on-device, however, but to be synced to a location that is available for anylsis in other locations - for instance, if I wanted to use an LLM to create a schedule of workouts, be able to push it directly to the backend from my laptop or desktop.

# App Requirements
1) Iphone only
2) Connectors to sensors like heart rate straps, tymewear breathing straps, my indoor trainer, etc
3) Notifications for things like fasting alerts, scheduled workouts, etc
4) Sync workouts/health data to and from apple fitness/health

# App Design
1) Homescreen with overview of metrics + quick actions perhaps? Maybe things like a button for start/stop fasting 
2) Navigation on the bottom for the categories - probably home, diet, exercise, health? Not sure what the best way to organize is yet
3) I'd like the app to be visually interesting, not a basic fitness app

# In-App Tools I would like to include
1) First tool will be a simple one, just a fasting tracker - can be as simple as a button and a timer
2) Second will be a workout calendar and tracked workouts, including sensors. We can start out with 4 types of workout plans - cycling, weight lifting, running, and mobility

# Desktop/browser application
1) Not sure if it should be browser based or native
2) A place to work on workout plans/schedules and analyze data locally
3) Potential LLM integration point for coaching/planning/analyzing
